items.title: Citations Made of Invisible Characters
items.content_text: An agent that reads the web and your files for you is only as useful as your ability to check it. "The record is 40.3°C" is a claim. "The record is 40.3°C", with a small badge that opens the Met Office page it came from, is something you can verify in one click. Suzent puts those badges inline, next to the sentence they support, in the desktop app, on your phone and in sub-agent reports. When the answer goes to Telegram or Slack instead, they turn into numbered references with a source list. This post is about how that works, and why the markers underneath are made of characters you are never meant to see. Ids come from the tools, not the model The easiest way to get bad citations is to let the model make them up. Ask a model to "cite your sources" and it will happily produce plausible URLs, footnote numbers that point nowhere, or a tidy list of sources at the end that it never actually read. So in Suzent the model never chooses what a source is. Every tool that brings in citable material, such as web search, page fetches, file reads, memory, browser pages and sub-agents, registers each source as it reads it and gets an id back, like t3_src_2 : the second source of the conversation's fourth turn. The tool prints that id right next to the evidence: [t3_src_2] Met Office: UK climate extremes The highest temperature recorded in the UK is 40.3°C, at Coningsby on 19 July 2022 … The model's job is narrow: when it states something from that result, it copies the id. If a tool result carries no label, the rules say not to cite it, and the same goes for the model's own reasoning or general knowledge. A badge in Suzent means "a tool really fetched this", never "the model felt like adding a reference". A few details make this hold up over a long conversation: - Ids carry the turn number , so a reply that cites something read three turns ago still resolves to the right page instead of colliding with this turn's first source. - The same page gets the same id. Reading a page twice reuses its id, so you don't get two badges for one source. - The source list is not in the prompt. Only the fixed citation rules are. The ids travel inside tool results, which are already part of the conversation, so the system prompt never changes between turns and stays in the provider's prompt cache. (That matters for cost. See how Suzent compacts context.) Why invisible characters The model then needs a way to write "this sentence comes from t3_src_2 " in the middle of its prose. The obvious options all collide with something: - [1] is ordinary Markdown and ordinary text. Papers, code and legal documents use it constantly. - [[t3_src_2]] looks like a wiki link, and Suzent's own memory notes are Markdown that might contain exactly that. - HTML tags or footnote syntax get mangled or rendered by the Markdown pipeline before the citation parser ever sees them. Unicode has a block made for exactly this situation: the Private Use Area , code points that no standard assigns any meaning to and that never appear in normal text. Suzent's marker is three of them wrapped around a type and a payload: U+E200 cite U+E202 t3_src_2 U+E201 This is the same style of marker that ChatGPT's own answers use. Because these characters never occur in real writing, a match can't be a false positive. The marker can't be confused with Markdown, code, a wiki link or a footnote in a document the agent is quoting. Several sources go in one marker ( t3_src_2 , t3_src_4 , separated by another U+E202 ), and the type keyword leaves room for other inline objects later without a new parser. The system prompt shows the model the exact characters to copy, and the renderer turns each marker into a badge. Models are messy, so the parser forgives That is the theory. In practice, models copy unusual characters imperfectly, and the text passes through browsers and Markdown renderers that have opinions about characters they don't recognise. Over time Suzent has learned to read six spellings of the same citation: What arrives Where it comes from --- --- U+E200 cite U+E202 t3_src_2 U+E201 the intended form [[cite:t3_src_2]] an ASCII form, handy for debugging and older output U+FFFC cite U+FFFC t3_src_2 U+FFFC some browser and Markdown paths swap private characters for the object replacement box cite:t3_src_2 the model kept the words but dropped the special characters citet3_src_2 the same, with no separator at all [t3_src_2] the model copied the tool's label instead of writing a marker The last two look a lot like ordinary text, so they only count when every id in them belongs to a real source in that conversation. A sentence that happens to contain [x_src_1] stays a sentence. All six render as the same badge. When a marker names an id that isn't in the current list, for example a source from an earlier part of the conversation, you get a muted badge instead of a broken one. When an answer has no sources at all, stray markers are removed rather than shown as boxes. Streaming without flicker Replies stream in a few characters at a time, so for a moment the screen holds half a marker: U+E200 cite U+E202 t3_sr . Shown as is, that is a row of tofu boxes that flicker into a badge a moment later. Both the desktop renderer and the backend hide a marker that has started but not closed, and show it only once it is complete. The markers that have no closing character at all, such as cite:t3_src_2 , are held back until the next bit of text shows where they end. Leaving the app Private Use Area characters are a good format between the model and Suzent's own renderer. They are a bad format anywhere else. Sent to Telegram, they show up as empty boxes. Pasted into an email, they mean nothing. So whenever an answer leaves for a surface that can't draw badges, such as Slack, Telegram, Discord, a message the agent sends on your behalf or an editor connected over ACP, Suzent rewrites citations into something portable: The UK's record is 40.3°C [1], set in July 2022 [1]. Sources: [1] Met Office: UK climate extremes — https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/… This also works while streaming. Text is converted as it arrives, the source list comes at the end, and as a last safety net any stray private character is stripped before it can reach an outside app. Two smaller boundaries get the same care: - Sub-agents. When a sub-agent researches something and reports back, its sources come along, renamed with a prefix of their own ( sa_…_src_1 ) so they can't collide with the main agent's own t3_src_1 . The main agent can cite the sub-agent's evidence directly, and the badge still opens the original page. - Truncation. When a long result has to be shortened, the cut never lands in the middle of a marker. Your own files count too Sources aren't only web pages. When the agent reads a file in your workspace, that file is a source. Its badge shows the file name with an icon for the file type, and clicking it opens the file on your computer. An answer about your project can point at the exact README.md or PDF it used, the same way an answer about the news points at a web page. What citations don't promise A badge says that a tool really fetched this source and that the model tied this sentence to it. It does not prove the sentence says exactly what the source says. Models can still overstate or misread. What citations change is how much work it is to catch that: one click, at the sentence where it happened. --- Web and sources · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: Long Conversations Without the Wait: How Suzent Compacts Context
items.content_text: Every agent that runs long enough meets the same wall. The conversation keeps growing, the model's context window does not, and at some point older messages have to be folded into a summary so the work can go on. This is called compaction , and nearly every agent harness does it the same way: wait until the window is almost full, stop, send the whole history to a model with "please summarize this", and swap the result in. That approach has three costs that are easy to miss: 1. You wait. Summarizing several hundred thousand tokens takes a while, and it happens right when you send your next message. 2. You pay full price to re-read everything. The summary request is a new, different prompt, so the provider's prompt cache does not apply. The entire history is billed again as fresh input. 3. You lose detail. A summary is lossy by design. Compact too early and the agent forgets things it still needed. Compact too late and it was already struggling to use them. This month we rebuilt Suzent's compaction around those three costs. Here is what changed and why. Write the summary from the cache Providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini and DeepSeek cache the beginning of a prompt they have seen recently. If your next request starts with exactly the same tokens, that part is read from the cache at a fraction of the normal input price. On Anthropic, for example, a cache read costs a tenth of the base price. A long agent conversation is almost entirely cache hits, because each request is the previous one plus a little more. The usual summary request throws that away. It flattens the history into text, wraps it in a new prompt, and sends it to a model, so nothing matches the cache. Suzent instead records each conversation's latest request exactly as it was sent : the same system prompt, the same tool definitions, the same messages in the same order. To write a summary, it sends that request again with one addition: the instruction to summarize, appended to the last message. To the provider, this looks like the conversation's next turn. The whole history is read from the cache, and only the instruction and the summary itself are billed at the full rate. The difference is large. Summarizing a 400k-token conversation on Anthropic used to cost 400k input tokens at the base price. Read from the cache, the same history costs about as much as 40k. Recording the request "as sent" matters more than it sounds. The framework adds small pieces to a request on the way out, so the history Suzent stores is not byte-for-byte what the provider saw, and a single differing byte early on is enough to miss the cache. When the recorded request no longer covers the history being folded, Suzent notices and falls back to the old method instead of writing a summary of the wrong messages. Prepare it before you need it Reading from the cache makes the summary cheap. It does not make it instant. So Suzent starts writing the next summary in the background, well before it is needed . Two thresholds do this, each a token count or a share of the model's window, whichever comes first: - Prepare at 350k tokens or 50% of the window. Suzent writes the summary in the background, during a long run or right after a reply finishes, while the cache is still warm from the request that just happened. - Compact at 500k tokens or 80% of the window. If a prepared summary matches the history, it is applied immediately. You do not wait for anything. A prepared summary is saved to disk, so restarting Suzent does not throw it away. If the conversation keeps growing a lot after the summary was written, Suzent writes a fresh one rather than applying a stale one. As far as we could find, no other agent harness pre-writes its compaction summary like this. Notice when the cache has gone cold Caches expire. Anthropic keeps one for 5 minutes by default (or an hour, at a higher write price), OpenAI and Gemini for roughly 5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, and DeepSeek for hours. No provider tells you how long an entry will actually live. That matters for a long conversation you come back to after lunch. If it is already at 400k tokens and the cache has expired, your next message re-reads all 400k at full price, even though compaction is not due yet. Suzent estimates each model's cache lifetime, starting from what the provider documents and raising the estimate whenever it sees a cache hit after a longer pause than expected. When you return to a conversation that is past the "prepare" threshold and the cache has probably gone cold, Suzent applies the prepared summary early . You send a much smaller prompt instead of paying to rebuild a cache for history that was about to be summarized anyway. When a summary has to be written on a cold cache, there is no discount to keep, so Suzent compares the price of the conversation's model with the memory extraction model and uses whichever is cheaper. Why 500k, and not 200k Our first version compacted at 200k tokens. It was cheaper, but compaction is lossy, and we were throwing away detail that many models could still use. On multi-needle recall benchmarks such as MRCR, where a model has to find several related facts scattered across a long context, the strongest current models hold up well to around half a million tokens and degrade noticeably after that. Several others fall off much earlier, near 200k. Past 500k, every message also pays to send the whole history again, cache or not. So the default is 500k tokens or 80% of the window, whichever comes first. A 128k model compacts at about 102k, a 200k model at 160k, and a 1M-token model at 500k. You can change both thresholds, or cap the context budget lower to keep costs down. You can see it happen A compaction shows up in the chat as a thin divider at the point where it happened, with the context size before and after. A line under it says whether the summary was prepared in advance or applied early because the cache had expired, and Show summary opens what the older messages became. The Context panel shows when the conversation was last compacted and whether the next summary is being prepared or is ready. None of this is magic, and you should not have to take it on faith. The summary is right there to read, and if it dropped something that mattered, you will know. --- Context and compaction settings · Configuration reference · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: Reach Your Agent From Anywhere, Through a Relay You Own
items.content_text: A personal agent that lives on your own computer has one obvious weakness: you are not always at your computer. You are on the train, at a café, or on mobile data, and the agent with your memory, your files and your projects is sitting at home behind a router that will not let anyone in. Most products solve this by putting the agent in their cloud. Then the question of reaching it disappears, along with the question of who owns it. Suzent now solves it differently. Your phone can reach the agent on your computer from any network, with no VPN, no port forwarding and no fixed IP address, through a relay that you deploy yourself . We do not run one. There is no Suzent server your conversations pass through, now or later. The usual options, and what each one costs Getting from a phone on mobile data to a computer behind a home router is an old problem with a few standard answers: - Port forwarding. Open a port on your router and point it at your computer. It works, but it puts a service on the public internet, many mobile and home networks block or share addresses so it fails anyway, and most people should not be configuring their router for an AI app. - A private network such as Tailscale. A very good option, and Suzent has supported it for a while. It does need the VPN app on every device and an account with the network provider, and it only helps devices you have added. A service like GitHub cannot call into it. - The vendor's relay. The easy path most apps take: the desktop and the phone both connect to the company's server, which passes messages between them. It just works, and it means a third party sits in the middle of every conversation you have with your agent, can see when you use it, and can switch it off. The third option is the one we did not want. Suzent's whole point is that the agent is yours: its memory is Markdown on your disk, its model is your choice, and its runtime is on your hardware. Routing every message through a server we operate would quietly undo that. So we kept the convenience of a relay and changed who runs it. How it works suzent-relay is a small open-source server. You deploy it once, either for free on Cloudflare Workers with no server to look after, or with Docker on any machine you already have. Suzent on your computer connects out to your relay and keeps that connection open. Because the connection goes outwards, nothing on your router has to change. When your phone sends a request to the relay, the relay passes it down that open connection, Suzent answers, and the answer travels back the same way. Ordinary requests, streamed replies and live connections all work, so chatting from your phone feels the same as at home. The relay keeps nothing on disk. The relay is a fork of alma-relay by yetone, an MIT-licensed relay with exactly the shape we wanted. Suzent adds its own encryption on top, described next. The relay cannot read your conversations A relay you deploy yourself is already much better than one run by a company. But a relay still runs on someone's infrastructure, such as a Cloudflare account or a rented server, so we did not want its safety to depend on that. Phone traffic is end-to-end encrypted , and the relay only passes on bytes it cannot read or change: 1. When you pair your phone, the QR code carries your computer's public key. The phone now knows exactly which machine it should be talking to. 2. Each time the phone connects through the relay, it runs a short handshake against that key (in the style of the Noise NK pattern, on P-256). Your computer has to prove it holds the matching private key before the phone sends anything. 3. Both sides derive fresh keys for that session, and every message is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and numbered. A message that is replayed, dropped or reordered fails to decrypt, and the session ends. A relay that tries to pretend to be your computer fails step 2. A relay that tries to tamper with a message fails step 3. The most it can do is refuse to pass traffic along, which you would notice. Two more rules keep the exposed surface small: - Only the phone channel and webhooks get through. Everything else in Suzent stays closed to the internet, relay or not. Requests that arrive through the relay are treated as remote callers, never as local ones. - The phone tries your direct addresses first. At home on Wi-Fi, or over Tailscale if you use it, the phone talks to your computer directly. The relay is only used when nothing closer answers. It also gives your webhooks an address Suzent can run a task when a webhook arrives: a new GitHub issue, a payment event, a form submission. Those services need a public URL to call, which a computer at home does not have. Once the relay is connected, every webhook task gets a second URL that goes through the relay. Give that one to GitHub and your agent picks up events wherever your computer happens to be. One honest caveat: the relay can read webhook payloads in transit, just as any webhook receiver can. That is one more reason for the relay to be yours. Setting it up 1. Deploy suzent-relay by following its README. Cloudflare Workers takes a few minutes and costs nothing for one person's traffic. Set a registration key so only your Suzent can use it. 2. In Suzent, open Settings → Devices → Relay , enter the relay address and registration key, and save. The status turns to Connected . 3. Turn on the background service, so Suzent stays connected after you close the desktop app. 4. Pair your phone by scanning a new QR code, which now includes the relay. A phone you paired earlier picks up the relay the next time it reaches your computer directly, for example on your home Wi-Fi. That is the whole setup. The full guide is in the relay documentation. Relay or Tailscale? Both are fine, and you can use both. The phone tries every address it knows. Tailscale is a great fit if you already use it: one private network for all your devices. The relay needs nothing on the phone beyond the Suzent app, works for anyone you hand a webhook URL to, and is a single small deployment you control end to end. What we will not do is offer a third option where the relay is ours. Your agent should be reachable from anywhere without anyone else being able to reach it, and the simplest way to keep that true is for the server in the middle to belong to you. --- Relay docs · suzent-relay · Mobile app · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: Suzent is now on the Microsoft Store
items.content_text: Suzent's Windows app is now on the Microsoft Store . Click Get and it installs: no PowerShell, no Git, no Python setup. It is the same agent as before, with the same memory, the same 16 model providers, and the same permission modes, in a package Windows manages for you. How to get it Open the Store listing, click Get , and launch Suzent from the Start menu. Add a model under Settings → Providers (or pick Ollama to stay fully local) and start chatting. The Quickstart covers the rest. The Store is now the recommended way to install on Windows. The desktop installer and the terminal script still work and are not going away. What's different about the Store build - Everything is bundled. The package carries its own Python runtime, Suzent and its dependencies, so the first launch does not download or build anything. - Sandboxed package identity. Windows installs it as a signed MSIX package and keeps the install folder read-only. Your chats, memory, settings and keys stay in ~/.suzent , so they survive reinstalls and uninstalls. - Updates come from the Store. Updates arrive through the Store like any other app. suzent update , upgrade and repair are turned off in this build because Windows owns the install. - Start at login, the Windows way. Settings → Background service turns on the package's startup task. It is off by default, and you can also manage it in Windows Settings → Apps → Startup. Nothing about how the agent behaves changes. Regent still runs your projects in the background and only comes back to you when a decision is yours. Risky actions still wait for your approval, under the rules you set. Already using the installer version? You can install the Store app next to it, and both use the same ~/.suzent . Run one at a time: quit the other one, including its background service, first. What's coming Store releases will follow the desktop release train: each tagged desktop release is submitted to the Store from CI, so the Store version keeps up with GitHub. Certification by Microsoft still applies, so expect a short delay after each release. --- Get it from the Microsoft Store · Quickstart · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: What Is Regent? Suzent's Orchestration Layer
items.content_text: The first time an AI agent finishes a real task for you, you give it a second one. Then a third. Within a week you have one session benchmarking a parser, another drafting a release post, a third triaging literature, and a fourth watching a deployment. You are no longer doing the work. You are doing something just as exhausting: you have become the router. Regent is Suzent's answer to that ceiling. Instead of facing a sidebar full of parallel sessions and polling each one yourself, you talk to a single orchestrator that dispatches work across your projects and only comes back when a decision belongs to you. Why "Regent"? Historically, a regent governs a realm in the monarch's stead — handling the day-to-day administration of state, coordinating ministers, and bringing only matters of sovereign consequence to the crown. In early builds of Suzent, this singleton chat was simply called SUZENT (and in the codebase it still lives in suzent.core.focal_agent , with the fixed chat ID focal-suzent ). As multi-project workflows matured, the generic name hid what made the role distinct: it is not "the main chatbot." You are the sovereign; Regent is the executive layer that governs your autonomous sessions while you focus elsewhere. What Regent actually is Instead of forcing you to act as a human router across a dozen tabs, Regent sits at the top of the desktop sidebar as a pinned card above your projects. Three strict rules define how it operates: 1. A single point of attention. You do not juggle tabs for Research , Coding , Writing , and Ops . You talk to Regent in one continuous conversation, and Regent routes work to the right project behind the scenes. 2. A dispatcher, never a doer. Regent does not write code, edit documents, or run shell commands. Those tools are stripped from its runtime policy. When you ask for project work, Regent uses agent_dispatch to wake or spawn a primary session inside that project — or hand the job to a configured coding agent over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). 3. A filter, not a relay. When a project session finishes or hits a blocker, it reports to Regent's inbox. Regent never dumps a 4,000-character execution log into your chat. It distills the outcome to a single sentence — or, if nothing needs your input, records the completion silently without notifying you at all. How is this different from sub-agents? If you have used sub-agents in coding tools (including Suzent's own explore , plan , write , verify , and web sub-agents), it is natural to ask: isn't Regent just a parent agent spawning sub-agents? No. They solve opposite problems at different layers of the stack: - Sub-agents protect an agent's context window. When a Coding session needs to grep 200 files or run a noisy test suite, it spawns an ephemeral explore or verify sub-agent via the agent tool. The sub-agent does one bounded job, keeps the raw tool output out of the parent's prompt, returns a summary to that parent session, and terminates. You still had to open the Coding session and tell it what to do. - Regent protects your attention. Regent sits above projects. It does not spawn throwaway workers for a single turn; it dispatches to durable Project Primary Sessions that own a folder, a context.md library, and a long-running task board — and those project sessions, in turn, spawn their own sub-agents while they work. Dimension Sub-agents ( agent tool) Project Primary Sessions Regent ( focal-suzent ) --- --- --- --- Core purpose Protect a session's context window & run parallel steps Execute durable work inside one project Protect your attention across all projects Scope Single task inside one parent session One project ( context.md , workspace, tasks) Every active project in Suzent Lifespan Ephemeral (one bounded job, folded under parent in sidebar) Long-lived conversation across days or weeks Permanent singleton pinned at the top of the sidebar Who talks to it Its parent project session Regent (via agent_dispatch ) or you directly You (and project sessions reporting back) Execution tools Scoped preset ( explore , write , verify , web ) Full project toolset (files, bash, MCP, sub-agents) None — orchestration & read-only lookup only Blocking behavior Can run synchronously or wake its parent session Pauses on ask_question , tool approvals, or blocked tasks Never waits on a turn; filters inbox events for you Put simply: a project session uses sub-agents to divide labor; you use Regent so you don't have to manage the project sessions. Filter, not relay Most multi-agent setups fail at the last mile: five agents do five things in parallel and then reward you with five walls of text to read. Regent's system prompt gives it a harder job: "You are a filter, not a relay." Every event that reaches Regent's inbox — a reply to a dispatched task, a session closing its last open task, or a task marked blocked on user input — passes through two branches: - If a session blocks on a decision , Regent surfaces one line: which project, what is stuck, and the exact choice it needs from you. - If a session finishes cleanly , Regent replies with the quiet token ( HEARTBEAT_OK ). The event stays in Regent's history so it can answer questions about it later, but no desktop notification fires and the unread badge does not move. Enforced boundaries, not polite prompts If you give an orchestrator agent a bash tool and a file editor, it will eventually stop orchestrating and start doing the work inline — polluting your main conversation with half-finished diffs and command output. Regent's boundaries are enforced in code before every turn ( apply_focal_tool_policy() ): - Write and execution tools are stripped. FOCAL_TOOL_NAMES equips only agent discovery/dispatch, memory/session search, web lookup, ask_question , read-only file tools, wake-up scheduling, and Regent's own notes tool. Every other tool is placed into denied_tools so it cannot even be discovered via tool search. MCP servers and working directories ( cwd ) are removed. - Zero-cost background check-ins. Regent runs a built-in 30-minute heartbeat to spot sessions that have stalled with open tasks (idle for 30+ minutes) or blockers you haven't answered in two hours. Before calling any model, Suzent hashes the current findings in Python ( should_run_focal_heartbeat() ): if nothing is stuck or the state hasn't changed since the last check-in, the turn is skipped in code. A quiet afternoon costs zero tokens. Project isolation without context bleed Because Regent never executes project work itself, each project keeps its own working directory, task list, and context.md cleanly separated. Your coding session's stack traces never leak into your research project's literature notes, and neither clogs your conversation with Regent. When you do want to inspect the raw work, Regent's board groups every project session by where it stands for you — waiting , running , idle , or resolved — and opening any session from the board gives you a one-click tag in the header to jump straight back to Regent. A COO, not another chat tab The right mental model for Regent is a Chief Operating Officer. You do not walk from desk to desk checking who is stuck; you state the objective once, let the teams work in their own rooms (with their own sub-agents), and expect to be interrupted only when a call is genuinely yours to make. Regent is a desktop feature today — the pinned sidebar card, the cross-project board, and the focal-suzent conversation live in the desktop app. The principle behind it is the core of how Suzent scales: sub-agents scale a session's execution; Regent scales your attention. --- Quickstart · Focal Agent Architecture · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: Your Agent, or Theirs?
items.content_text: Somewhere in the last year, "personal AI agent" stopped being a category in a pitch deck and became a thing normal people are told they should want. In 2026 it is not one product but a whole shelf of them, each promising the same thing with different branding: an assistant that knows you, that works while you sleep, that handles your email and your calendar and — soon, they all say, in the next update — the boring parts of your life. The pitch is seductive because it is close to something real. An agent that actually knows you is genuinely more useful than one that does not. That is not marketing; it is how context works. The question is what that usefulness is built on, and who it ultimately serves. This post is not another "big tech is evil" list. Every product below solves a real problem for real people. But every one of them also sits on the same unspoken architecture, and it is worth understanding that architecture before you hand it the contents of your life. First, what a personal agent actually is The word has been stretched until it barely means anything, so a short taxonomy helps. - A chatbot answers what you ask, then forgets. No memory, no initiative. - A copilot assists inside a specific context — an editor, a spreadsheet — and disappears when you leave. - An agent has memory (it remembers), authority (it acts — runs tools, sends things, changes state), and continuity (it keeps running without you standing over it). - A personal agent is the agent aimed at you rather than at a business workflow: your inbox, your calendar, your files, your life. It is the difference between a tool you point at a task and a system you point at your week. The defining property is not intelligence. It is persistence plus authority . An agent that cannot act is a chatbot with better recall. An agent that cannot remember is a script. The entire 2026 crop is betting that the combination — persistent and trusted to act — is the next platform. The 2026 lineup Here is who is selling you an agent this year, in rough order of when they showed up. Vendor Product Announced What it runs on The pitch --- --- --- --- --- Anthropic Claude Cowork Feb 2026 Cloud Automates business workflows; the launch wiped roughly $285B off SaaS, IT, and legal market caps Apple Siri (Apple Intelligence) 2026 On-device-first The private upgrade: your iPhone does it locally Microsoft Copilot 2026 Cloud A "three-horizon AI architecture" rebuilt across Windows and Microsoft 365 Meta Muse Sep 8, 2026 Cloud The most-downloaded app on arrival; performs tasks on your behalf and expanded to small-business agents within weeks OpenAI Dots Sep 29, 2026 (DevDay) Cloud (GPT-6 Astra) Always-on personal agents with avatars, working across ChatGPT, Slack, and Teams Google Gemini Spark I/O 2026 Cloud (Gemini 3.5 Flash + Antigravity) A 24/7 agent that drafts email, watches your inbox, files things, pulls PDF data into Sheets — and, they say, will eventually spend your money Two patterns jump out. First, the timeline is accelerating : what the enterprise world took a couple of years to adopt, the personal-agent market compressed into about nine months. Second, the direction of every pitch is identical. The more of your data the agent can touch, the more "useful" it is described as being. That is the load-bearing fact, and every vendor says it like it is a feature rather than a dependency. "Your agent" — a short translation guide Each word in the marketing does real work. It is worth knowing what it is doing. You hear Which means What it does not say --- --- --- "Your agent" The account remembers you, in the vendor's database You do not own the thing that remembers "Memory" A vector store on their servers, tuned to serve you better Readable, portable, editable? No such claim is made "Works for you" Executes inside their sandbox, through their integrations Whose rules define the limits? Their terms of service "Private" Encrypted at rest and in transit, with the operator able to read it as needed "Private from other users" is not the same as "private from the operator" "On-device" (Apple) Inference runs locally on your hardware The memory and identity still sync back into the account by default None of this is a lie. That is the tricky part. "Private" and "memory" and "works for you" are all true in the sense the vendor means them. The misdirection is in what the sentences leave out — specifically, who can read, move, edit, and survive the thing that knows you. The real question: integration versus sovereignty Every honest framing of this market keeps coming back to the same fork: > Are you willing to integrate all of your data more tightly into one > company — or do you keep it for yourself? This is not abstract. Everything the agent does well — deduplicating your inbox, anticipating your schedule, filing your receipts — is powered by integration : the more of your life flows into one graph, the smarter the agent becomes about you. Integration is genuinely what makes these products feel magical. That is the honest case for the big-vendor agent, and it is a good one. The honest case for the other side is that integration and ownership sit on the same axis, and they point in opposite directions. Every degree you deepen the integration, you deepen your dependence on whoever holds the graph. The agent that knows you best is, by construction, the one you can least afford to lose — and the one with the most complete picture of you. You cannot optimize for both at full throttle. You can have a maximally helpful agent, or a maximally yours agent, and you have to choose how far to lean. What sovereignty offers is not more convenience — it is the option to say no, without having to start over. There is a sane middle path This does not have to be a clean either/or, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of dishonesty. The useful distinction is between the engine and the vehicle . - The engine is the model — the intelligence. That can be rented. Frontier models are genuinely, measurably better at many things, and there is no shame in using them. - The vehicle is your agent — its memory, its skills, the rules of what it may do, its identity, where it lives. That is what should be yours . A sovereign agent that calls GPT, Claude, or Gemini through an API keeps cutting-edge capability while holding memory, permissions, and identity on your side of the line. You rent the engine; you own the vehicle. That configuration is what most people actually want, and it is what Suzent is built to be: memory as files you own, any model you choose, and explicit permission rules with human approval gates. Four questions to ask before you hand one over Whatever you pick, these cut through the copy. If you cannot answer them, you do not yet know what you are buying. 1. Can I read all of its memory — in a plain format I can open? Not a settings preview. The whole thing. 2. Can I edit or delete what it believes about me? Or is my only recourse telling it nicely and hoping the correction sticks? 3. Can I disable, approve, and audit what it is allowed to do? Or is "what it may do" a sentence in a terms-of-service I accepted once? 4. If the vendor disappears, shuts down, or triples the price — does my agent survive? Or was the agent actually a rental dressed as a companion? A personal agent is going to become the most intimate software you own — more so than your email, your browser, maybe your phone. It will know what you decided, what you abandoned, what you are afraid to admit you keep putting off. The only question that ever really mattered, and the one this post keeps circling, is the one you should sit with before you click past the next changelog: Are you willing to integrate it — all of it, more tightly every year — into one company? Or do you keep it for yourself? --- Quickstart · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: Swap the Model, Keep the Agent
items.content_text: A useful way to tell whether you own an AI agent: change the model underneath it and see what happens. If the agent forgets who you are, loses its instructions, or has to be reconstructed from scratch, then its identity was never in the parts you controlled. It was in the vendor's product, and you were borrowing it. If the agent keeps working — same memory, same skills, same boundaries, same accumulated understanding of your projects — then the model was doing what a model should do: thinking, not being . {/ truncate /} The model is an engine, not the self This is the first condition of agent sovereignty, and it is the one people find least intuitive, because the model is the impressive part. It writes the words. It does the reasoning. Surely that is the agent? But consider what actually distinguishes your agent from an identical installation belonging to someone else. Same code, same model, same version. The difference is entirely in: - what it remembers about you and your work, - the skills you gave it, - the workspace and files it can reach, - the permissions and rules you set, - the conventions it has learned not to violate. None of that is in the model. All of it is in state that can live on your side of the line. The model supplies capability; the state supplies identity. Swap the first and the second is untouched — provided the architecture kept them separate in the first place. That is why Suzent supports many providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, Ollama and local models, and others — and lets you switch per session rather than per installation. What has to be true for the swap to be cheap "Model-agnostic" is a claim a lot of tools make. Three things determine whether it survives contact with a real migration. Memory has to be model-independent. If what the agent knows is stored as embeddings from one provider's model, switching means re-embedding everything, and any drift in retrieval quality is invisible until it bites. Suzent's source of truth is Markdown; the semantic index is derived from those files and can be rebuilt. Changing the embedding model is a reindex, not a data loss. Skills have to be prose, not prompts tuned to one model. Suzent skills are Markdown knowledge modules describing how to work in a domain. Documentation transfers between models. Brittle prompt scaffolding tuned to one model's quirks does not. Capability differences have to be handled, not ignored. This is the honest caveat. Models genuinely differ — context windows, tool-calling reliability, vision support, instruction-following under long autonomous runs. A swap is a config change, but it is not a no-op . A smaller local model will not carry a long agentic task the way a frontier model does. Sovereignty gives you the freedom to choose; it does not make the choices equivalent, and any project telling you otherwise is selling something. What this buys you day to day Model independence sounds like insurance against a rare disaster. In practice it pays out constantly, in ordinary ways: - Run a cheap fast model for routine work and a frontier model for hard problems, in the same agent, with the same memory. - Move sensitive work to a local model without moving to a different tool or losing context. - Adopt a new release the week it ships instead of waiting for a vendor to integrate it. - Stop caring, structurally, about which lab is currently ahead. That last one is the real dividend. When identity is independent of the model, the frontier race becomes something you benefit from rather than something you are exposed to. The check Question two of the sovereignty test: can I replace the model without resetting its identity? It is worth actually trying, rather than trusting the marketing copy. Point your agent at a different provider and ask it something only your agent would know. The answer tells you where its identity was living all along. --- Providers · What makes an agent sovereign · Source

items.title: What Happens to Your AI Agent When the Provider Shuts Down
items.content_text: Shutdowns make the argument vividly, but they are the rare case. The common case is quieter and happens constantly: a model you depended on is deprecated, a price tier changes, a product is folded into another product, a rate limit arrives, terms are revised, a feature you built a workflow around is retired. The interesting question is not whether that happens. It is what it costs you when it does — and that is decided long before, by where your agent's durable parts live. {/ truncate /} Two versions of the same bad Tuesday Suppose the provider behind your agent announces a sunset in ninety days. If your agent is an account , the ninety days are a migration project. The accumulated context — everything it learned about your work — is in a database you can query only through whatever export the vendor offers, in whatever shape they offer it. Custom instructions have to be rewritten for a different product with different conventions. Integrations have to be rebuilt against different APIs. And the new agent starts at zero: it does not know your projects, your preferences, or the eleven things you already told the old one not to do. The cost is not the subscription. It is the re-accumulation. If your agent is a system you own , the ninety days are a config edit. The memory is Markdown in a directory you control, unchanged. The skills are your own Markdown modules, unchanged. The permission rules are yours, unchanged. You point at a different provider, and the agent that knows your work continues knowing it. What you lost was an API key. The boundary that decides which Tuesday you get The distinction is not paranoia about vendors and it is not a bet on which company survives. It is a structural question you can answer in advance: > Which parts of this agent could the provider take away, and which parts are > already mine? For a sovereign AI agent, the answer is drawn deliberately: - Memory — Markdown files on your disk, readable and versionable. - Skills — knowledge modules you author, in your own directory. - Configuration and permissions — rules you wrote, stored locally. - Workspace — folders and sandboxes you granted. - The model — rented, deliberately, and replaceable. Everything above the last line is yours regardless of what happens to the company below it. That is what the fifth question of the sovereignty test is checking: can the agent survive the disappearance of its provider? Continuity is a design decision, not a promise It is worth being precise about what makes this work, because "we will never shut down" is not a plan and no vendor can honestly offer one. Continuity comes from two properties, both of which are architectural: Identity is not in the model. If what makes the agent yours is its memory, skills, and workspace rather than a specific set of weights or a specific vendor's fine-tune, then models become interchangeable engines. Suzent supports many providers and lets you switch per session precisely so that no single one becomes load-bearing. State is portable without secrets. Moving an agent should not mean moving your credentials. Suzent's sync design carries configuration, skills, and Markdown memory to a private repository while keeping API keys, device identity, and the local secret store off the wire entirely. Neither of these is exotic. Both have to be decided early, because retrofitting portability onto an agent whose memory is a proprietary blob is not a small change — it is a rewrite. The unglamorous version of the advice You do not need to predict which provider will falter. You need your agent's answer to one question to be yes: If this provider vanished tonight, would I still have the agent tomorrow? Keep the memory in files you can open. Keep the permissions in rules you wrote. Keep the credentials separable from both. Then a sunset notice is an inconvenience rather than an eviction. --- Read the sovereignty protocol · Quickstart · Source

items.title: How to Own Your AI Agent's Memory
items.content_text: Memory is the part of an AI agent that is genuinely yours, in the sense that it could not have come from anywhere else. The model is a commodity — impressive, interchangeable, and someone else's. What your agent knows about your projects, your preferences, and the decisions you already made is not. Which makes it worth asking where that lives, and on whose terms. {/ truncate /} Three questions that decide ownership Whatever agent you use, memory is ownable to the degree that you can answer yes to these: Can you read all of it? Not a summary, not a settings screen showing the last twenty items. The whole thing, in a format you can open. Can you change it? Agents form wrong impressions. If the only correction mechanism is telling the agent it was wrong and hoping the correction sticks, you do not have edit access — you have a suggestion box. Can you take it with you? To another machine, another tool, another decade. If the answer requires the vendor to still exist and still offer an export endpoint, that is a conditional yes, which is a no. Most hosted agent memory fails at least two of these, usually the second and third. Not maliciously — opaque memory is just the path of least resistance when you are building a product and memory is an implementation detail. What ownable memory looks like The design that satisfies all three is unglamorous: plain text files on a filesystem you control. Suzent's memory is Markdown. After an exchange, it picks out what is worth keeping — a preference, a project detail, a fact — and appends it to that day's log. Overnight, a consolidation pass folds those logs into topic pages, merging duplicates and resolving contradictions. The consequences of that being files rather than rows are practical: - You can read it. Open the directory. It is a folder of Markdown. - You can edit it. Fix a wrong fact in your editor. Delete the page about the project you abandoned. The agent's next read sees your version. - You can version it. Put the memory directory under Git and you have full history, diffs of what your agent learned this week, and the ability to revert a bad consolidation pass. - You can move it. Copy the folder. That is the migration. - You can grep it. Every tool you already own works on it. There is a semantic index for retrieval, because search over a year of Markdown needs one. The important architectural commitment is the direction of authority: the index serves the files, and can be rebuilt from them. Delete the index and nothing is lost. Delete the files and the index is meaningless. That ordering is what keeps the memory yours rather than the database's. The memory documentation covers the capture and consolidation mechanics in detail. The parts that should not be portable One caveat worth stating, because "own your memory" invites an obvious mistake: not everything the agent holds should travel with it. API keys, provider credentials, device identity, and the local secret store are deliberately excluded from portable state. When Suzent syncs to a private Git repository, the payload builder rejects those paths before push. Memory and skills move; secrets stay on the device. This matters because the failure mode of naive portability is a memory folder that quietly accumulates credentials and then gets pushed somewhere. Ownership means being able to move the agent without moving your keys. Why this is the first sovereignty question Of the five questions in the sovereignty test, memory is first, because it is the one that decides whether the others can even be asked. If memory is portable and readable, swapping models is a configuration change — identity lives in the files, not the weights. If memory is portable and readable, a provider shutting down costs you an API key. If it is not, then every other form of independence is theoretical: you can leave any time you like, as long as you are willing to start over. Start with the memory. The rest follows from it. --- Memory docs · Quickstart · Source

items.title: Sovereign AI Agent vs Cloud AI Assistant
items.content_text: A cloud AI assistant is a product you log into. A sovereign AI agent is a system you own: its identity, memory, skills, workspace, and runtime are governed by you rather than by a model provider or platform. The difference is not local versus remote, and it is not open source versus closed. It is about which side of the boundary the durable parts live on. Here is the comparison without the marketing. {/ truncate /} Where each one keeps the things that matter Cloud AI assistant Sovereign AI agent --- --- --- Memory Vendor database; readable through a UI, exportable in part Files on your disk; readable, editable, versionable in Git Identity Coupled to the vendor's model and product decisions Held in memory, skills, and workspace, independent of the model Model choice Whatever the vendor ships, when they ship it Any provider, or a local model; swappable per session Permissions Vendor-defined; you accept or decline the whole product Rules you write, per tool and per scope, with approval gates Execution Vendor's sandbox, vendor's integrations Your machine, your folders, your approved devices Continuity Ends when the account, product, or terms end Survives providers, models, and machines Setup cost Sign up Install, configure keys, choose your boundaries Maintenance None, by design Yours Default quality Tuned end to end by a large team Depends on the model and configuration you choose The honest case for the rented option The last three rows are not throwaways, and a comparison that pretends otherwise is not worth reading. Hosted assistants are genuinely easier. Someone else handles model upgrades, infrastructure, safety tuning, and the thousand small integration details that make a product feel finished. For a great many uses — drafting, summarizing, answering questions, the occasional bit of research — that convenience is worth far more than ownership of the transcript, and paying for it is a perfectly sensible decision. Sovereignty has real costs. You choose the model, which means you can choose badly. You set the permission boundaries, which means you can set them wrong. Nothing upgrades itself unless you decide it should. If the agent is a convenience rather than infrastructure, that overhead may simply not be worth carrying. When ownership starts to matter The calculus changes as the agent accumulates two things: context about you and authority to act . Context compounds. An agent that has watched you work for a year knows your projects, your conventions, the things you have already decided and do not want re-litigated. That is expensive to rebuild and impossible to rebuild exactly. When it lives somewhere you cannot read or move, you are one policy change away from starting over. Authority is sharper. An assistant that suggests text is a different proposition from an agent that runs commands, edits files, sends messages, and acts on a schedule while you sleep. Once an agent can do things, the question of who defines the limits stops being philosophical. Suzent's answer is explicit permission rules with human approval gates; a hosted product's answer is its terms of service. If your agent has both — deep context and real authority — then "the vendor could change this" is a live operational risk rather than an abstract one. The test that separates them The useful question is not which category a product claims. It is what happens under pressure: 1. Can you inspect, edit, version, and delete its memory? 2. Can you replace the model without resetting its identity? 3. Can you define, approve, and audit what it is allowed to do? 4. Can you move its state without exporting your credentials? 5. Can the agent survive the disappearance of its provider? A cloud assistant answers "partly" to the first and "no" to the rest. That is not a defect; it is what being a hosted product means. But it tells you exactly what you are choosing. The full version of the test, and what each answer implies, is on what makes an agent sovereign. Not actually either/or Worth saying: these are not mutually exclusive. A sovereign agent that calls GPT, Claude, or Gemini through an API gets frontier model quality while keeping memory, skills, and permissions on your side of the boundary. You are renting the engine, deliberately, while owning the vehicle. That combination — any provider you like, memory in your own files — is the configuration most people actually want, and it is what Suzent is built to be. --- Quickstart · Source (Apache-2.0)

items.title: Sovereign AI for Individuals, Not Nations
items.content_text: Search for "sovereign AI" and you will find nations. Countries building domestic model training capacity, governments procuring GPU clusters they control outright, regulators drawing borders around where citizen data may be processed. The word means something specific there: a state that does not need another state's permission to compute. That is a real and important use of the term. It is also not the only scale at which the idea makes sense. {/ truncate /} The same argument, one person wide Strip the national framing away and the argument underneath is simple. A capability you depend on, which someone else can revoke, price, or redefine without asking you, is not really yours. Nations noticed this about model infrastructure. The same thing is true of the AI agent that reads your notes, remembers your projects, and increasingly acts on your behalf. A sovereign AI agent is an AI agent whose identity, memory, skills, workspace, and runtime are owned and governed by its user rather than by a model provider or platform. Its durable state lives in files you can read, edit, version, and move. Its actions run inside permission boundaries you define. And replacing the underlying model does not reset the agent that knows your work. Nations want sovereign AI so a foreign vendor cannot switch off their compute. You want a sovereign agent so a vendor cannot switch off your memory. It is the same objection at a different scale. What you actually rent today Most people's "AI assistant" is an account. Consider what that means concretely: - The memory of your past conversations lives in a database you cannot read, export in full, or correct. - The assistant's personality and instructions are configured through a form whose behaviour changes when the vendor updates the model beneath it. - Its ability to act on anything — files, email, calendars — exists only through integrations the vendor chose to build and can retire. - If you stop paying, or the vendor changes terms, or the product is discontinued, the accumulated context is gone. Not degraded. Gone. None of that is scandalous. It is the normal shape of a hosted product, and hosted products are often the right trade. But it is worth naming plainly, because the thing being accumulated in that account — a model of how you work — is unusually expensive to rebuild. Sovereignty is not the same as self-hosting The most common misreading is that sovereignty means running something on your own hardware. Local execution is part of it, but it is neither sufficient nor the whole point. You can run a model locally and still have a non-sovereign agent: if its memory is an opaque binary blob, if its identity is welded to the specific model weights you happen to be running, if there is no way to inspect or constrain what it does with your filesystem, then "local" bought you privacy but not ownership. Conversely, an agent can call a hosted frontier model over an API and remain sovereign, provided the parts that constitute the agent — memory, skills, configuration, permissions, workspace — stay on your side of the line. The model is an engine. Engines are replaceable. That is the point. Agent sovereignty has four conditions: 1. Sovereign mind — the model is an engine, not the self. 2. Sovereign authority — autonomy operates under rules you write. 3. Sovereign vessel — the runtime is a domain you control. 4. Sovereign continuity — the agent outlives any platform it ran on. Each is spelled out, with a five-question test for checking whether any given agent actually meets them, on what makes an agent sovereign. Why the distinction matters now Agents are crossing from answering to acting. An assistant that drafts a paragraph and an agent that files the expense report, pushes the commit, or sends the message are different kinds of thing to hand your life to. The second kind accumulates a great deal of context about you, and exercises a great deal of authority on your behalf. The moment to decide who holds that context and that authority is before it is substantial enough to be painful to lose. Nations arrived at this conclusion about compute. The version for individuals is smaller, cheaper, and considerably easier to act on: keep the agent's memory in files you can open, keep its permissions in rules you wrote, and make sure you could move both tomorrow. --- Suzent is an open-source, local-first implementation of that idea. The quickstart takes about five minutes, and the source is Apache-2.0.

items.title: Suzent Mesh: A Nervous System for Your Sovereign AI
items.content_text: A truly Sovereign AI cannot be confined to a single silicon cage. If Suzent is your digital extension, it needs the ability to project its will and perception across the entirety of your hardware domain. We are not building another cloud SaaS orchestration tool. We are building a decentralized nervous system for your personal AI. We call this architecture the Suzent Mesh . At the core of this matrix is the Node System . {/ truncate /} Escaping the Sandbox: What are Nodes? In the Suzent paradigm, your primary agent is the "Mind," and Nodes act as its sensory organs and actuators scattered across your network. Inspired by OpenClaw's distributed control philosophy, the Node system shatters the traditional local-sandbox limit. It allows your agent to seamlessly reach across the network to execute commands, read environments, or borrow compute power from other devices you own. Currently, the Mesh is forging a unified cluster out of your primary workstations: - Peer PC/Mac/Linux Rigs : Link your devices so the agent can traverse them. Your lightweight laptop agent can seamlessly read files from your home server, trigger heavy bash scripts on your Linux rig, or deploy a localized agent instance on a remote desktop. - (The Horizon) Mobile & IoT Endpoints : Soon, the Mesh will extend to smartphones and ambient devices, transforming them into remote eyes and ears ( camera.snap , location.get ) for your sovereign agent. The Architecture: A Hub-and-Spoke Matrix At its foundation, the Mesh operates on a low-latency, WebSocket-based JSON-RPC protocol. 1. The Core (NodeManager) : Your primary Suzent Server acts as the central dispatcher. 2. The Synapses (Nodes) : Devices establish secure WebSocket tunnels ( ws:// : /ws/node ) to the core. 3. The Handshake : Upon linking, a node declares its identity, platform, and a strict manifest of capabilities (commands it authorizes the core to invoke). 4. Invocation : When your agent decides an action must happen elsewhere , the NodeManager dispatches the command matrix to the target node, executing it natively on the remote hardware. Zero-Trust Sovereign Boundaries Power requires absolute control. Permitting an AI to execute code across your network demands a paranoid, scope-gated security model. We do not route your telemetry through corporate cloud relays. - Loopback Trust : The local app ( 127.0.0.1 ) operates with native authority. - Node Scope ( node ) : Gained via a physical operator-approved pairing ritual. It grants WebSocket presence but zero HTTP access . - Agent Scope ( agent ) : The "Control Grant." This permits a remote peer only to trigger an isolated /chat session on the target device. - Full Scope ( full ) : A heavily guarded, revocable host token minted exclusively for total remote API operation. Peer Control: Machine Telepathy For devices running full Suzent environments, the Mesh unlocks something profound: Peer Control . Instead of treating a remote PC as a dumb terminal, Suzent treats it as a peer intelligence. You can grant one device permission to drive the agent of another. - Local Discovery : Suzent actively sweeps your domain via mDNS (LAN) and Tailscale (cross-network) to find dormant peer nodes. - The Grant : You issue a cryptographic control-grant. The target operator approves, forging a durable, secure link. - The Trigger : Your local agent can now stream prompts, context, and even file attachments to the remote agent. The Result: You are working on a thin ultrabook in a coffee shop. You ask your Suzent agent to analyze a massive local dataset. Recognizing its limits, your local agent delegates the task to the Suzent agent running on your water-cooled workstation at home, streaming the analytical thoughts and results back to your laptop in real-time. Speaking A2A: The Open Door Peer Control is powerful, but on its own it is a closed federation — Suzent talking to Suzent. A sovereign network whose only citizens are copies of itself is not sovereign. It is just a smaller walled garden. So the Mesh also speaks A2A (Agent2Agent) — the open agent-interoperability standard now governed by the Linux Foundation. Not a Suzent dialect. The actual protocol, JSON-RPC over HTTP, verified in our test suite against the reference SDK client. This is a deliberate division of labor, and it mirrors how MCP and A2A divide the world: Layer Protocol What it talks to --- --- --- Tools MCP Services and capabilities your agent uses Devices Suzent Nodes Your hardware — transparent, enumerable capability manifests Agents A2A Other intelligences — opaque execution, standard wire Nodes are deliberately not being folded into A2A. A node publishes exactly what it can do ( camera.snap , system.script ); A2A's entire premise is opaque execution, where you delegate a goal and never see inside. Those are different contracts, and collapsing them would destroy the manifest that makes nodes useful. Discovery Is Ours; Reach Is Theirs A2A defines four ways to find an agent: a well-known URL, a curated registry, direct configuration, and an authenticated extended card. Notably, there is no global public directory of A2A agents , and the spec contains no LAN discovery at all. That is precisely where the Mesh earns its keep. Suzent finds peers on your own network with zero configuration, via mDNS and Tailscale — something the standard cannot do. A2A then gives those findings somewhere to go beyond your own hardware. - Your card : Each device can publish an Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json — its name, its OS environment, its skills, and how to authenticate. It is off by default . Publishing announces that you exist; it authorizes nothing. Execution still requires a grant you approved by hand. - Their card : Paste any A2A agent's URL. Suzent fetches the card, confirms it is real, and adds it to the Mesh next to your own devices. Tasks That Can Ask You Questions Real delegation is not fire-and-forget, and this is where the open standard bought us something our own protocol could not express. A2A models work as a task with a genuine lifecycle: submitted → working → completed , but also failed , canceled , and the interesting one — input-required . A remote agent that hits an ambiguity can stop and ask , and the task waits. > legal-review · input-required > "Which jurisdiction should I assume?" Your Mesh shows that question, you answer it inline, and the same task resumes — because the reply carries the task's ID. A one-shot "send a message, stream a reply" channel simply has nowhere to put that pause. Every delegated task is visible in the Mesh with its live state, and can be refreshed or canceled mid-flight. The Result: the coffee-shop scenario, but the workstation at home is no longer the only possible destination. Your agent can hand the statistical modeling to a specialist agent that a colleague runs, receive a clarifying question back, answer it, and stream the result home — without either side having ever heard of the other's framework. Tap into the Mesh The Mesh is already active in the CLI. You can view your network matrix and trigger remote executions immediately: Scan your sovereign network suzent node list Inspect a node's declared capabilities suzent node describe "Home-Server-Alpha" Command the remote node suzent node invoke "Home-Server-Alpha" system.script run="deploy.sh" Any A2A client can reach a device that has published its card: Read a Suzent device's Agent Card — the standard discovery path curl https://your-device:25314/.well-known/agent-card.json You can inspect and drive the open half of the Mesh from the Mesh tab in Settings: your own Agent Card and its publish switch, every Suzent peer and external A2A agent side by side, and the live state of every task in flight — in either direction. The Sovereignty Continues The Suzent Mesh is the death of the isolated terminal. Nodes give your agent hands across your own hardware; A2A gives it a voice among agents you did not build. Sovereignty was never about isolation. A system that can only talk to itself has not escaped the cage — it has just decorated one. Real sovereignty is owning your side of an open protocol: your keys, your hardware, your rules, and no vendor's permission needed to speak to anyone. As we extend the Mesh to mobile endpoints and deepen our A2A support, your personal AI will cease to be just an app on your screen. It will become a unified, ambient intelligence that surrounds you—entirely owned by you, serving only your laws, and able to negotiate with the wider world on equal terms.
